options: The object's data and the behaviors that operate on that data are combined into a single, self-contained unit.
The object's data is stored in a global table that any code can read and write.
The object inherits all its behaviors from a parent class.
The object is compiled into a separate binary from the rest of the program.
questions.explanation: Weisfeld defines encapsulation as the mechanism that binds together the data (attributes) and the code (methods/behaviors) that acts on the data, keeping both safe from outside interference and misuse.

questions.prompt: A class makes all its attributes private and exposes only the operations other objects truly need. Which OOP principle is this primarily demonstrating?
options: Multiple inheritance
Information hiding
Method overloading
Garbage collection
questions.explanation: Weisfeld stresses that information hiding is the practice of hiding the internal structure and implementation details of an object: only the public interface is exposed, and attribute values are only changed via that interface.

questions.prompt: Why does Weisfeld say the object-oriented 'thought process' requires thinking at a higher level of abstraction?
options: Because object code runs faster than procedural code.
Because design models abstract away implementation details and represent the system as interacting objects.
Because compilers refuse to build procedural code.
Because abstraction removes the need for requirements.
questions.explanation: The book's central premise: with OOP you first think in terms of the problem space — identifying objects, their responsibilities, and their interfaces — rather than diving straight into implementation details like you do with a procedural, top-down approach.

questions.prompt: Weisfeld argues that a well-designed object should:
options: Delegate all its work to a central controller object.
Be responsible for itself, carrying its own data and the behaviors that act on it.
Expose all attributes publicly so other objects can manage them.
Avoid interacting with any other object in the system.
questions.explanation: A core guideline of thinking in terms of objects: each object should be responsible for itself — its own data and behavior — and interact with other objects only through well-defined public interfaces.
questions.sourceChapter: Ch. 2 — How to Think in Terms of Objects

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an accurate distinction between an interface and an abstract class?
options: An abstract class can contain implemented behavior and state, while a traditional interface provides no implementation at all.
An interface can contain constructors, while an abstract class cannot.
You can instantiate an abstract class but not an interface.
There is no difference — they are interchangeable in every language.
questions.explanation: In Weisfeld's treatment of frameworks and reuse, an abstract class can provide a partial implementation (fields, implemented methods) that subclasses build on, whereas a classic interface is a pure contract with no implementation. A class can also implement many interfaces but typically inherit only one class.
questions.sourceChapter: Ch. 8 — Frameworks and Reuse: Designing with Interfaces and Abstract Classes

questions.prompt: What happens if code tries to create an instance of an abstract class?
options: It works — abstract classes are just regular classes with extra features.
It fails: abstract classes cannot be instantiated; they must be subclassed by concrete classes.
It works only if the abstract class has a default constructor.
It works only inside the same package or namespace.
questions.explanation: An abstract class is a template for other classes. It cannot be instantiated directly because it may declare operations that have no implementation; concrete subclasses fill those in.
questions.sourceChapter: Ch. 8 — Frameworks and Reuse: Designing with Interfaces and Abstract Classes

questions.prompt: A Dog class is designed to extend an Animal class. Which relationship does this model?
options: has-a
is-a
uses-a
knows-a
questions.explanation: Inheritance models the is-a relationship: a Dog is an Animal. Weisfeld covers inheritance as the primary mechanism for expressing is-a and generalization/specialization hierarchies.

questions.prompt: A Car class holds references to Engine and Wheel objects to do part of its work. Which relationship and mechanism is this?
options: is-a, via inheritance
has-a, via composition
is-a, via polymorphism
has-a, via method overloading
questions.explanation: Composition expresses the has-a relationship: a Car has an Engine and has Wheels. Weisfeld treats inheritance and composition as the two fundamental ways classes relate, and devotes a chapter to choosing between them.

questions.prompt: According to Weisfeld, when the relationship between two classes is NOT a true is-a relationship, what should you generally prefer?
options: Inheritance anyway, since it reuses the most code.
Composition, because forcing is-a semantics breaks the model and couples classes tightly.
Global variables, so both classes can share state.
Copy-pasting the code between the two classes.
questions.explanation: A classic guideline from the book: use inheritance only when a genuine is-a relationship exists; otherwise composition (possibly with delegation) is the better, more flexible design.

questions.prompt: The same message sent to objects of different classes results in each object executing its own appropriate behavior. This is:
options: Static binding
Polymorphism
Serialization
Encapsulation
questions.explanation: Polymorphism literally means 'many forms': identical interface, different behavior. Weisfeld shows that a single object can take on many forms, and a single message can invoke different implementations depending on the receiving object's actual class.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between method overloading and method overriding?
options: Overloading reuses a method name with different signatures in the same class (compile-time); overriding redefines a superclass method in a subclass (runtime).
Overriding creates new method names; overloading renames existing ones.
They are identical — the terms are synonyms.
Overloading only happens in interfaces; overriding only happens in abstract classes.
questions.explanation: Overloaded methods share a name but differ in parameter lists and are resolved at compile time. Overriding replaces a parent class's implementation of the same signature in a subclass and is resolved dynamically at run time — a key mechanism behind polymorphism.

questions.prompt: Why does Weisfeld advise keeping coupling between classes as low as possible?
options: Low coupling makes it possible to change one class without breaking others that depend on it.
Low coupling reduces the size of compiled binaries.
Low coupling guarantees zero bugs in the codebase.
Low coupling increases the number of classes you must modify for each change.
questions.explanation: Coupling is the degree to which one class depends on another. Tightly coupled classes must be understood, tested, and changed together; loose coupling keeps designs flexible and maintainable, which is why class design guidelines push toward minimizing it.

questions.prompt: A class named FileManager also sends marketing emails and computes payroll. From a class-design standpoint, what is wrong?
options: Nothing — bigger classes are always better.
It has low cohesion: it packs unrelated responsibilities into one class instead of a single, focused one.
It violates the rule that all methods must be static.
It is missing a UML diagram.
questions.explanation: Cohesion measures how focused a class's responsibilities are. A class should do one thing well — the file manager should manage files. Unrelated responsibilities belong in separate, highly cohesive classes.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a static attribute or method from an instance one?
options: A static member belongs to the class itself and is shared by all instances, not stored per object.
A static member can only be accessed from inside a constructor.
A static member exists only while a single object is alive.
A static member is always private in every language.
questions.explanation: Weisfeld introduces static (class-level) members alongside instance members: a static attribute is shared by all objects of the class, and a static method can be invoked through the class without any instance.

questions.prompt: Why does Weisfeld recommend accessor and mutator methods (getters/setters) rather than exposing attributes directly?
options: They let the class validate changes, hide the internal representation, and preserve the public interface even if the storage changes.
Getters and setters run faster than direct field access.
They are required by every compiler.
They eliminate the need for encapsulation entirely.
questions.explanation: Accessors/mutators enforce information hiding: the class controls how its attributes are read and written, can validate inputs, and can change its internal storage later without breaking every caller.
